speaker: Patient
text: 59-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset sensation that the room is spinning, leading to several episodes of nausea and vomiting. The symptoms started as he was going to bed and lasted for approximately 3 minutes. He mentions that he has never experienced anything like this before and currently feels at his baseline.

speaker: Doctor
text: Since your symptoms resolved quickly without lingering hearing issues, did you notice if the spinning sensation was triggered by specific head movements, like rolling over in bed or looking up? Also, have you had any recent headaches, vision changes, or difficulty walking since the episode?

text: Past medical history: The patient is otherwise healthy with only a history of eczema. No prior episodes of similar nature. Social history: No significant social history provided.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your history of eczema and no other medical issues, I need to confirm if the spinning returned immediately when you moved your head after the initial episode, and did you feel any weakness or numbness in your limbs during the event? speaker: Patient
text: Denies headaches, hearing loss, tinnitus, loss of consciousness or neurological deficits.

speaker: Doctor
text: Since you denied neurological deficits and hearing loss, I need to know if the dizziness recurs specifically when you roll over in bed or look up, which would suggest a positional cause. REQUEST TEST: Dix-Hallpike maneuver.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Dix-Hallpike Manoeuvre: Positive, inducing nystagmus and reproducing patient’s symptoms of vertigo when head is turned to the left and laid back. Additional findings: Physiologic nystagmus observed with severe symptoms and notable nystagmus when head is turned to the left and laid back. Head Imaging: Normal, with no evidence of stroke or masses. Audiometry: Within normal limits for age.

speaker: Doctor
text: The positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver combined with your normal hearing and imaging strongly points to Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
